source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Dueling Lines: Wedge Pullback to the Trend Line

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: DuelingLinesPullbackEnd
candidates.quote: A pullback in a bull trend always ends at a support level, and a pullback in a bear trend always ends at a resistance level, and therefore all pullbacks are dueling lines patterns.
candidates.description: A pullback ends where two independent lines coincide at the same price near the current bar -- e.g., the pullback's own (falling) trend channel line intersecting the larger trend's (rising) trend line, or the trend line coinciding with a horizontal swing level or the moving average -- which increases the odds the pullback reverses back into the larger trend's direction there.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context/confluence filter feeding a with-trend pullback-end entry)

complexity.reason: needs trend-line and trend-channel-line projection from swing pivots plus tracked support/resistance levels (horizontal swing points, moving average) and a price-proximity test between them

notes: Shared primitive for this chapter; Brooks says ALL pullbacks technically qualify, he just reserves the term for cases where the trader can actually see the confluence -- treated here as a detectable/tunable-tolerance condition rather than a universal truth.

candidates.name: DuelingLinesWedgeConfluenceEntry
candidates.quote: The most reliable form is when the pullback is in a channel and it has a wedge shape or three pushes, and the signal bar for the end of the pullback is a bar that pokes through the trend line and reverses.
candidates.description: The most reliable dueling-lines setup: the pullback itself has a wedge/three-push shape inside a channel, and its signal bar pokes through the major trend line intraday and then closes back on the trend side of it, right where the pullback's own channel line and the major trend line intersect.
candidates.pseudocode:
isReliableDuelingLinesSignal = isWedgeBottom[1] && isDuelingLinesConfluence[1]
   && low[1] < majorTrendLinePrice[1] && close[1] > majorTrendLinePrice[1]; // signal bar pokes through the trend line intrabar and closes back above it
enterLongNextBarOpen = isReliableDuelingLinesSignal
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the signal bar's high

complexity.reason: composes two hard pivot/line-based primitives plus a poke-through-and-close-back test on the signal bar

candidates.name: SteepPullbackRequiresSecondEntry
candidates.quote: Since the move down to bar 6 was steep, it was reasonable to wait for the second entry at the bar 7 higher low, buying on a stop at one tick over its high.
candidates.description: When the countertrend pullback leg into a dueling-lines confluence is steep, skip the first reversal signal and wait for a second entry (e.g., a subsequent higher low), buying a stop one tick above that second signal bar's high.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the second signal bar's high

complexity.reason: pullback 'steepness' has no stated numeric test; needs a design decision (e.g., points-per-bar slope or trend-bar fraction) before it can be coded

notes: The higher-low signal-bar detection and the gap-avoidance stop-entry form reuse the same pattern as R18-02/R18-06 from chapter 18.

candidates.name: HorizontalSupportDuelingLinesDoubleBottom
candidates.quote: The support line could be a horizontal line, like across a prior swing low, and this could set up a double bottom buy signal as the wedge is ending.
candidates.description: When the long-term support at a dueling-lines pullback end is a horizontal line across a prior swing low, the pullback's low can print near that same level, forming a double bottom that adds to the trend-line confluence buy signal.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the second bottom's signal bar high

complexity.reason: needs both the dueling-lines confluence primitive and a double-bottom price-proximity test against a stored prior swing low

notes: Double top/bottom is the subject of chapter 20 (not yet mined at the time this file was written); the dedup pass should merge this with whatever double-bottom primitive chapter 20 defines.

candidates.name: BearTrendDayOpenNearHighCloseNearLow
candidates.quote: Even though it was a trading range day, it appears as a bear trend day on the daily chart because it opened near the high and closed near the low.
candidates.description: On a daily bar, a session that opens near its high and closes near its low reads as a bear trend day on the daily chart, even if the intraday action was actually a trading range.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (daily-bar shape classification, a context filter for higher-timeframe bias)

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic on that bar's own open/high/low/close, structurally identical to the corpus's existing close-range-position rules

notes: Not a duplicate of CloseRangePosition (that rule only tests where the close sits in the bar's range); this one additionally tests where the open sits, and is meant for a daily bar.

rejected.quote: The goal is to look at the overall shape and then choose any trend channel line that contains the price action. Then, watch how the market reacts after penetrating the line.
rejected.reason: pure discretion ("look at the overall shape and choose"), no bar-level test specified

chapter_summary: Chapter 19 names the confluence of a pullback's own trend channel line with a larger trend line (or a horizontal swing level or moving average) as a 'dueling lines' pattern, and argues the most reliable version combines this confluence with a wedge/three-push pullback shape (composing chapter 18's wedge primitive). It adds a steep-pullback second-entry filter, a horizontal-support double-bottom variant, and, in a chart aside, a simple open-near-high/close-near-low daily-bar test for 'bear trend day' shape. Short chapter (2 pages, 3 figures), mostly one extended chart discussion; all candidates here are context filters or composite entries rather than standalone triggers.
